source.title: Don't Decay the Learning Rate, Increase the Batch Size
source.authors: Samuel L. Smith; Pieter-Jan Kindermans; Chris Ying; Quoc V. Le

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper directly tests large-batch schedules against learning-rate decay and shows conditions where test accuracy is similar, slightly lower, or clearly lower. This refines the large-batch penalty claim in V5.
record.gate_note: The paper reports learning curves, test accuracies and update counts for alternative batch-size and learning-rate schedules. Cited findings from earlier studies are not recorded as rows. Figure-only learning curves are not transcribed into numerical rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly tests V5's recipe-adaptation qualification: increasing batch size during training can preserve held-out accuracy at the same epoch budget, while some more aggressive schedules lose accuracy. It is not an original source listed for V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that replacing learning-rate decay with batch-size increases often preserves training and test curves at the same epoch budget while reducing updates. Learning-rate and momentum scaling permit further update reductions, but higher momentum can reduce accuracy. They demonstrate faster ImageNet training by converting existing schedules without additional hyperparameter tuning.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies replacing learning-rate decay with batch-size increases, plus scaling batch size with learning rate or momentum; it is not a direct test of the original fixed-batch large-batch penalty protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with optimizer and schedule: increasing momentum to 0.98 lowers CIFAR-10 test accuracy; on ImageNet, the first-step batch increase has a slight accuracy drop; keeping batch size at 16384 throughout while doubling initial learning rate reaches 75.0% rather than 76.1%.
record.problems: The study reports only two runs for the Inception-ResNet-V2 ImageNet schedule comparison and notes noisy test curves due to fewer evaluations. Several curves are available only as figures and have no exact accuracy values in the text. The paper does not test the fixed-epoch large-batch penalty across language models or workload-dependent batch thresholds.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible result rows omitted. Figure-only learning-curve points were not numerically reconstructed.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and local connectivity.
Comparative held-out performance of adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Language models, systematic workload-dependent batch thresholds, longer-training remedies, and isolated effects of warmup or normalization changes.
Measured magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.

missing.what: Appendix B's initial-learning-rate sweep reports median accuracy over five runs per point: proportional batch scaling preserves performance only up to approximately 0.4, beyond which accuracy falls. Section 5.2 describes this sweep as holding batch size constant, contradicting Appendix B's explicit proportional-scaling description; retain that discrepancy.
missing.locator: Appendix B, Figure 8; Section 5.2 final paragraph

record.verdict_notes: States describe the presence of an accuracy penalty; an absent penalty under adaptation can support V5 because adaptation is explicitly part of that version. The Figure 7 momentum inconsistency prevents assigning reliable exact coefficients to its higher-momentum results.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization under different tuning conditions.
Language models; fixed-epoch comparisons across workload-dependent batch thresholds; comparisons to all cited adaptation methods.
Sharpness or other measured properties tracking the generalization gap.
Removal of memorized examples and resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: 16-4 wide ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Increased momentum coefficient and batch size while increasing initial learning rate.
rows.uncertainty: Median accuracies across five additional runs: 94.3% and 93.5%, respectively
rows.note: The schedule used less than 2500 updates; authors describe a lower test accuracy.

rows.subject: Inception-ResNet-V2
rows.operation_detail: Compared fixed batch size with learning-rate decay against a batch-size increase at the first step, followed by learning-rate decays.
rows.uncertainty: Difference described as similar to variance between training runs

rows.check: The small numerical penalty is reported correctly, but only two runs per schedule were performed and the authors say the difference is comparable to run variation. It is not an established robust penalty.

source_check.problem: The numerical decrease supports partial only descriptively; the authors say its size is comparable to variation between runs.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Increased batch size after the first 30 epochs to use the full TPU pod.
rows.baseline: 76.1% with batches of 8192 in under 45 minutes
rows.note: This is a same-accuracy result after adapting batch size during training, not a fixed-epoch comparison.
rows.check: Correct the note: this is a fixed-epoch comparison, with both schedules using 90 epochs. The adapted run uses the full TPU pod after epoch 30; the fixed-8192 baseline uses half a pod.

source_check.correct: Both schedules train for 90 epochs. Fixed batch 8192: half TPU pod, 256 tensorcores, 76.1%, under 45 minutes. Adapted schedule: batch 8192 for 30 epochs, then batch 16384 using the full TPU pod for 60 epochs, 76.1%, under 30 minutes.
source_check.problem: The adapted run uses the full pod after epoch 30; the note incorrectly denies that this is a fixed-epoch comparison.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Doubled initial learning rate and used batches of 16384 throughout training.
rows.baseline: 76.1% for increasing batch size during training
rows.note: The authors present this as evidence that increasing batch size during training matters for the performance gains.
rows.check: The 1.1-point penalty is clear, rather than merely partial. The fixed-8192 baseline also achieves 76.1%, providing a direct smaller-batch comparison at 90 epochs. Doubling the learning rate does not remove the penalty.
